articleHtml:
By David Vance, Senior Financial Modeler · Last updated: November 27, 2026

Why time matters more than the rate

Compound interest means you earn returns on your earlier returns. In the first years the effect looks small. In later decades it does most of the work. This page uses a single set of numbers, a $10,000 start and $500 a month at a 7% annual return, to show what changes the outcome most: time, fees and inflation.

Important: 7% is an assumption for illustration, not a prediction or a promise. Real returns vary year to year and can be negative.

The formula

With regular deposits: FV = P(1+r)^n + PMT × [((1+r)^n − 1) ÷ r], where P is the starting amount, PMT is the monthly deposit, r is the monthly rate (annual rate ÷ 12) and n is the total number of months. The calculator above applies this and charts each year.

Worked example: $10,000 plus $500 a month at 7%

YearsYou contributedBalanceGrowth earned
10$70,000$106,639$36,639
20$130,000$300,851$170,851
30$190,000$691,150$501,150
40$250,000$1,475,521$1,225,521

After 10 years, growth is about half of what you put in. After 30 years it is more than two and a half times your contributions. The last 10 years (from year 30 to 40) add roughly $784,000, more than the first 30 years combined.

The cost of waiting 10 years

Take two savers who both invest $400 a month at 7% until age 65. One starts at 25, the other at 35.

  • Start at 25 (40 years): contributes $192,000, ends with about $1,049,900.
  • Start at 35 (30 years): contributes $144,000, ends with about $488,000.

The early starter put in $48,000 more and finished with about $562,000 more. The extra decade is worth more than the extra money. If you are older than 25, the lesson is not despair; it is that every month you start earlier helps, and increasing the monthly amount can make up part of the gap.

Fees: a small percentage that costs a lot

A 1% annual fee sounds minor. Take the same 30-year example and reduce the return from 7% to 6% to reflect it:

  • 7% (no fee drag): $691,150
  • 6% (after a 1% fee): $562,483

That 1% costs about $128,700, or nearly 19% of the final balance. Check the expense ratio of any fund, and any advisory fee, before you invest. Low-cost index funds exist partly for this reason.

Inflation: the number that matters is real return

Prices rise over time, so a dollar in 30 years buys less than a dollar today. If inflation averages 3%, a 7% nominal return is roughly a 4% real return. Running the same example at 4% gives about $380,200 after 30 years in today's purchasing power, compared with the nominal $691,150. When you plan for a goal such as retirement, use an inflation-adjusted figure.

The Rule of 72

Divide 72 by the annual rate to estimate the doubling time. At 7%, money doubles in about 72 ÷ 7 ≈ 10.3 years. With annual compounding the exact figure is 10.24 years, so the shortcut is close. It also works for debt: 18% credit card interest doubles what you owe in roughly four years if you only make small payments.

Compounding frequency: monthly vs annual

More frequent compounding helps slightly. $1,000 at 8% for 10 years grows to $2,158.92 compounded annually and $2,219.64 compounded monthly. The gap of $60 is much smaller than the effect of rate, time or fees. Do not choose an account on compounding frequency alone.

Paying off debt versus investing

Paying off a loan is a guaranteed return equal to its interest rate. Clearing a 6.5% loan is like earning 6.5% with no risk. When your debt rate is higher than the return you can reasonably expect, repayment often wins. When it is much lower, investing may come out ahead, but returns are not guaranteed. A balance between the two is common, and the right mix depends on your risk tolerance and emergency savings.

Common mistakes

  • Treating an illustrative 7% as a promise.
  • Ignoring fees and taxes on returns.
  • Forgetting inflation when setting a target.
  • Stopping contributions in market downturns, when deposits buy more units.
  • Confusing the nominal rate with the effective annual rate when comparing accounts.

Frequently asked questions

How does compound interest differ from simple interest?

Simple interest is earned only on the original amount. Compound interest is earned on the original amount plus all interest already added, so growth accelerates over time.

How do monthly deposits affect compound growth?

Each deposit starts earning returns from the month it is made. Regular deposits usually contribute more to the final balance than the starting amount over long periods.

What is the Rule of 72?

It is a shortcut: divide 72 by the annual return percentage to estimate how many years it takes money to double.

Is a 7% return realistic?

It is a common planning assumption for long-term diversified stock investing before inflation, but actual results vary widely and are not guaranteed. Use lower and higher scenarios to test your plan.

Methodology and sources

All results use the formula above with monthly compounding and deposits at the end of each month. They exclude taxes, fees (unless stated) and inflation (unless stated). This is not investment advice; past returns do not guarantee future results. For general investor education see Investor.gov. Corrections: support@smartcalclab.com.
